slides.title: Learning Objectives
slides.text:
Learning Objectives

•  Define path planning and explain why it matters for robot safety,
   efficiency, and autonomy.
•  Describe the robot planning architecture (perception, localization,
   planning, plan execution).
•  Distinguish global planning from local (reactive) planning.
•  Represent an environment using occupancy grids and graph-based
   maps.
•  Explain the graph search problem, including frontier
  and explored sets.
•  Compare Breadth-First Search (BFS), Uniform-Cost
   Search (UCS), and A*

slides.title: What Is Path Planning?
slides.text:
What Is Path Planning?
Definition:
   Process of determining an optimal and
    feasible collision-free route from the start
    (initial configuration) to goal (desired
    configuration) for a robot in the
   environment.

The Core Challenge:
   The robot must navigate safely while respecting
    physical constraints (e.g., size, speed limits, turning
    radius).



                                                                                                           4

visualInspection.notes: Dashed start-to-goal route avoids three labeled rectangular obstacles. Definition includes feasible, collision-free, optimal route between configurations; size, speed and turning radius constraints. Picture does not establish numerical optimality or finite-footprint clearance. Footer 4.

slides.title: Path Planning
slides.text:
Path Planning

Why Does It Matter?
•  Safety: Prevents damage to the robot and its environment.
•  Efficiency: Saves time, battery life, and computational power.
•  Autonomy: Enables robots to operate in unpredictable, real-world
   environments without human intervention.





                                                                                                           5

visualInspection.notes: Safety, efficiency and autonomy bullets; factory aisle photograph is illustrative, with no algorithm trace or quantitative output. Claims describe aims, not guarantees in arbitrary unknown environments. Footer 5.

slides.title: Path Planning
slides.text:
Path Planning

Key components:
•   Start & Goal Configurations: Defining where the robot start and final destination.
•  Environment Representation: Creating a digital map of obstacles and free space.
•  Robot Constraints: Accounting for physical limits (kinematics and dynamics).
•  Path Selection Criteria: Optimizing for path length, smoothness, or energy
    efficiency.

Advanced Applications:
     •  Surveillance & Monitoring.
     •  Search & Rescue.
     •   Logistics & Delivery.
     •  Exploration.


                                                                                                            6

visualInspection.notes: Four components: start/goal configurations, obstacle/free-space map, kinematic/dynamic constraints, objective criteria length/smoothness/energy; four application categories surveillance, rescue, logistics, exploration. Footer 6.

slides.title: Role of Path Planning in Different Domain
slides.text:
Role of Path Planning in Different Domain
•  Drones (UAVs):
   – Environment: 3D aerial navigation.
   – Key Challenge: Path planning around high-altitude obstacles, and restricted zones.
   – Example: Autonomous drone delivery or structural inspection.
•  Manipulators (Robotic Arms):
   – Environment: Fixed-base operation with multi-axis movement.
   – Key Challenge: Moving the end-effector while obeying kinematic and dynamic
        constraints.
   – Example: Passing a cup of coffee smoothly without spilling.
•  Mobile Robots:
   – Environment: Navigates complex indoor and outdoor space.
   – Key Challenge: Dynamic obstacle avoidance.
   – Example: Self-driving cars navigating city traffic.


                                                                                                             7

visualInspection.notes: Three prose domains: UAV 3D obstacles/restricted zones and delivery/inspection; fixed-base multi-axis arm constraints and smooth coffee passing; mobile dynamic-obstacle traffic navigation. No numerical trajectories. Footer 7.

slides.title: Robot Planning Architecture
slides.text:
Robot Planning Architecture

                   Localization
•  The robot estimates its exact position relative to
  the map.
•  Answers: "Where am I on this map?"
•  Uses tools like: GPS, IMU, wheel encoders, and
  SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping).

                      Perception
•  The robot converts sensor data into a map of obstacles.
•  Answers: "What does the world around me look like?“
•  Uses tools like: Ultrasonic Sensor, Camera, LiDAR, and
   Radar.


                                                                                                           9

visualInspection.notes: Two boxed prose panels separate map-relative localization (GPS, IMU, encoders, SLAM) from obstacle perception (ultrasonic, camera, LiDAR, radar). Word exact overstates estimation certainty. Illustration pose panel has X=4.87 m,Y=-1.95 m,Z=0.12 m; yaw=115.4°,pitch=0.1°,roll=0.0°, point-cloud labels. Small coordinate triad appears to label two axes Y; do not derive a valid frame from this illustration. Footer 9.

slides.title: Path Planning: Global vs. Local Planning
slides.text:
Path Planning: Global vs. Local Planning

After localization, we reach the Planning phase, where algorithm decide the safest
route.
•  Global Planning: Uses a complete, pre-existing map of the environment to
   compute an optimal path offline in advance (before movement starts).
•  Local Planning(reactive navigation): Uses real-time sensor data to avoid nearby
   obstacles and adjust the path dynamically online (during movement).





                                                                                                          10

visualInspection.notes: Global whole-map/offline versus local live-sensor/online contrast; route map A to B with magnified car steering around a pothole. Offline/complete map are this comparison's simplifying assumptions, not universal necessary conditions for global planning. Footer 10.

Path Planning: Global vs. Local Planning

       Global Path Planning                      Local Path Planning
•  Plan whole path from start to        •  Short-term path planning for immediate
   goal point.                               collision avoidance.
•  Full knowledge of map.               •  Detect real-time data from sensors.
•  Obstacle (fixed) are known in        •  Excellent reactive behavior.
  advance.                                •  Avoid dynamic obstacle.
•  Poor adoptability to dynamic         • Run constantly while robot is moving.
  change in environment.
•  Execute algorithm prior to start   Advanced robot
   (offline).                      combine both to
• Common algorithm: Dijkstra’s or   reach safely to goal
   A-star                              destination.

visualInspection.notes: Side-by-side global/local comparison: known fixed map, poor dynamic adaptation and Dijkstra/A* versus immediate sensor-reactive dynamic avoidance during movement; box recommends combining both. Page adds hybrid architecture emphasis beyond prior slide. Footer 11.

slides.title: Representation of environment (Map)
slides.text:
Representation of environment (Map)

•  To plan a path inside for robot, we need a map
   representation that robot can search.
1.  Occupancy-grid maps
•  An occupancy grid divides the environment into a grid of
   (usually square) cells. Each cell holds a binary value
   describing whether it is:
   – 0 (free): the robot can enter this cell, or
                                                                        Grid map   – 1 (occupied): an obstacle; the robot cannot enter.
•  Pros: simple to implement and easy to understand.
•  Cons:
   – High memory for large environment.
   – Precision limitation due to grid resolution.


                                                                                                          12

visualInspection.notes: Binary occupancy map 0 free/1 occupied; 8x8 figure. Black cells by row: r1 c6,c7,c8; r2 c4,c6; r3 c1,c2; r4 none; r5 c4,c5,c6; r6 c1,c4,c5; r7 c4; r8 c4,c8 (16 occupied,48 free). Resolution versus memory trade-off. Binary map is simplified; robot footprint and unknown-cell policy are not supplied. Footer 12.

slides.title: Representation of environment (Map)
slides.text:
Representation of environment (Map)

2.  Graph-based maps
•  Represent the environment as a graph G=(V,E) of
   key locations (vertices) and their connections with
   edges
   – Vertices (nodes) V: representing recognizable
       places (e.g. "kitchen," "living room" connected
      by a doorway).
   – Edges E: representing routes between places,
      each with an associated cost (distance, time,
        fuel, etc.).
•   It is similar to a subway map.
•  Pros: effective for a large-scale environment.
•  Cons: less detailed about the physical layout.

                                                                                                           13

visualInspection.notes: Graph definition G=(V,E), recognizable places and costed routes; subway-map analogy, scale efficiency/detail trade-off. Directed figure edges A→B3,A→C1,C→B7,B→D5,C→D2,B→E1,D→E7. Labels B Central Park Hub,C River Crossing,D Industrial District. No units for these figure weights. Footer 13.

slides.lectureTitle: Path planning, Graph Searches, and the A* Algorithm
slides.title: Representation of environment (Map)
slides.text:
Representation of environment (Map)
•  Number on the edges are called edge weights.
•   It act as the "cost" or "friction" of traveling
   between two nodes.
•  Instead of treating every connection equally,
   edge weights help algorithms determine the
   absolute best path based on real-world
   constraints.
•  Depending on application, edge weights can
   represent several different factors:
    – Most straightforward weight is physical distance (e.g.,
        kilometers or miles) between two nodes.
    –  In navigation apps, weights often represent estimated
        travel time rather than distance.

                                                                                                            14

visualInspection.notes: Same directed five-node graph and weights as p1100. Edge weights may encode distance,time,fuel; best path depends on chosen cost model. Absolute best wording needs qualification rather than all-objective guarantee. Footer 14.

slides.lectureTitle: Path planning, Graph Searches, and the A* Algorithm
slides.title: Representation of environment (Map)
slides.text:
Representation of environment (Map)

•  While grids and graphs are typically treated as distinct map
   representations, they can be easily converted to allow
   grid-based environments to be searched using standard      4-Connected
   graph algorithms.
•  The conversion process involves placing a vertex in every
   grid cell and adding edges to connect it to reachable
   neighboring cells.
•  Edge Costs based on Connectivity:
                                                                                    8-Connected
   – 4-Connected: Neighbors share an edge (Up, Down,
        Left, Right). Moving to any neighbor has an edge cost
       of 1.0.
   – 8-Connected: Neighbors share an edge or corner
       (adds 4 diagonals). Vertical/horizontal moves cost 1.0,
       diagonal moves cost  2 ≈1.414.


                                                                                                            15

visualInspection.notes: Actual figures show center with four edge-sharing neighbors or eight edge/corner neighbors. Printed diagonal cost has radical √2≈1.414 (text extraction loses radical). Unit cardinal cost1; grid-to-graph conversion must respect reachable/free cells. Corner-cutting policy and finite footprint are not specified. Footer 15.

slides.lectureTitle: Path planning, Graph Searches, and the A* Algorithm
slides.title: The Graph Search Problem
slides.text:
The Graph Search Problem

If we want to travel from a start vertex (A) to a goal vertex (E) through a graph.


 Naive strategy:
    – Randomly hop between neighboring vertices.
    – Might eventually reach the goal.
  Cons:
    – There is no guarantee of reaching the goal,
    – The path found would almost certainly not be
        optimal.





                                                                                                            16

visualInspection.notes: Random-hop prose says no guarantee and almost certainly nonoptimal. The actual repeated A→E directed graph is acyclic and every branch ends at E, so following outgoing edges reaches E in at most four moves. Generic warning must not be applied unqualified to this displayed DAG. Uniform neighbor choice is not supplied, but can be an explicit generated assumption for probability questions. Footer 16.

slides.lectureTitle: Path planning, Graph Searches, and the A* Algorithm
slides.title: The Graph Search Problem
slides.text:
The Graph Search Problem
•  Definitions:
    ➢Frontier: the set of vertices we know about and are scheduled to explore, but
       haven't explored yet.
   ➢Explored set: vertices we have already expanded and are finished with.
 General algorithm:
 1.   Initialize frontier with the start vertex.
 2.  Repeat:
    – Pick a vertex from the frontier (different algorithms pick differently).
    –  If it's the goal, stop.
    – Otherwise, expand it: add its unexplored neighbors to
       the frontier, and move it to the explored set.
 3.    If the frontier becomes empty, and the goal was never
     found, it means no path exists.


                                                                                                          17

visualInspection.notes: Generic search initializes start frontier, selects vertex, tests goal before expansion, otherwise adds unexplored neighbors and closes it; empty frontier implies no path in exhaustively searched represented graph. Does not explicitly spell out duplicate-frontier handling or weighted relaxation; qualify these with later UCS example. Footer 17.

slides.title: Example: Autonomous Vehicle Path Planning
slides.text:
Example: Autonomous Vehicle Path Planning

➢In regional planning and logistics, finding the most efficient route between
   geographically separated municipal zones is a fundamental challenge.
•  Consider a delivery network consisting of seven municipal zones, designated
   as Zone A through Zone G. An autonomous logistics vehicle must travel from its
   starting depot in Zone A to a final distribution hub in Zone G.
•  The road connections between these zones have varying lengths (travel costs), and
   geographic constraints prevent direct roads between zones.





                                                                                                           18

visualInspection.notes: Seven municipal zones A–G with undirected unweighted topology AB,AC,BD,BE,CF,DE,EF,DG,FG. Goal A→G; geographic constraints exclude other direct roads. Existing two approved items cover graph description and absent edge. Footer 18.

slides.lectureTitle: Path planning, Graph Searches, and the A* Algorithm
slides.title: Example: Autonomous Vehicle Path Planning
slides.text:
Example: Autonomous Vehicle Path Planning

Problem Objectives: To analyze different algorithm for path planning.

1.   Breadth-First Search (BFS): Identify the path using a purely
     topological, hop-minimizing approach. Determine the total
     travel distance of the resulting path.
2.  Uniform-Cost Search (UCS): Find the mathematically
     shortest path based on actual road distances. Track the
     step-by-step state of the prioritized frontier and the final
      list of explored zones.
3.  A* Search: Incorporate the straight-line heuristic distance
    to guide the search.
Compare the number of expanded zones to the previous
algorithms to evaluate the search efficiency gains.



                                                                                                          19

visualInspection.notes: Comparison objectives explicitly distinguish BFS hops, UCS weighted shortest path/frontier trace, A* straight-line guidance and number of expansions as search-efficiency metric. Existing two approved questions cover these objectives. Footer 19.

slides.lectureTitle: Path planning, Graph Searches, and the A* Algorithm
slides.title: 1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)
slides.text:
1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

•  Breadth-First Search (BFS) is a systematic
   graph search algorithm used in robot
   navigation to find a path between two
   points on a graph-based map.
•  Data Structures: It uses a FIFO (First-In,
   First-Out) queue to manage the
   "frontier" (the open set of scheduled
   vertices) and an "explored" set (the
   closed set of visited vertices) to prevent
   backtracking.
•   It ignores the actual weight (distance) on
   the edges, effectively treating all edge
   costs as equal.



                                                                                                          20

visualInspection.notes: FIFO frontier and explored/closed set; BFS ignores edge weights. Existing three approved items cover queue, open/closed and topology-order invariance. Possible distinct grid synthesis: equal cost versus diagonal-weighted BFS optimality. Footer 20.

slides.printedNumberEvidence: Extracted from actual bottom-right footer region; not inferred from physical page.

slides.title: 1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)
slides.text:
1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Step-by-Step Execution
•   Initialize:
   –  Frontier: [A]
   – Explored: []
•  Step 1: Expand A. Add its
   neighbors B and C to the frontier.
   –  Frontier: [B, C]
   – Explored: [A]
•  Step 2: Expand the first node in the
   queue, B. Add its unvisited
   neighbors D and E.
   –  Frontier: [C, D, E]
   – Explored: [A, B]

                                                                                                          21

visualInspection.notes: BFS start frontier[A],closed[]; expand A→[B,C],closed[A]; expand B→[C,D,E],closed[A,B]. Existing two items cover initialization and trace. Footer 21.

slides.title: 1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)
slides.text:
1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Step-by-Step Execution
•  Step 3: Expand C. Add its unvisited
  neighbor F.
   – Frontier: [D, E, F]
   – Explored: [A, B, C]
•  Step 4: Expand D. Add its unvisited
  neighbor G (the goal).
   – Frontier: [E, F, G]
   – Explored: [A, B, C, D]
   – The goal G is now generated on the frontier.




                                                                                                          22

visualInspection.notes: Expand C adds F: frontier[D,E,F],closed[A,B,C]; expand D adds G but not already queued E: frontier[E,F,G],closed[A,B,C,D]. Goal generated but not yet popped. Existing two items cover steps; duplicate-frontier treatment implicit. Footer 22.

slides.lectureTitle: Path planning, Graph Searches, and the A* Algorithm
slides.title: 1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)
slides.text:
1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

•  Pros: Very simple to implement.
   Finds the path with the minimum
  number of transitions/hops (3 hops
  A→B→D→G).

•  Cons: Physically suboptimal.
  Because it ignores road lengths, it
  chooses a longer route (cost of 17)
  over a much shorter alternative
   (cost of 9).




                                                                                                          24

visualInspection.notes: BFS pros simple/minimum hops and source example physical-distance suboptimality17 versus9. Existing assertion-reason item covers that specific distinction; do not universalize all BFS outputs as suboptimal. Footer 24.

slides.lectureTitle: Path planning, Graph Searches, and the A* Algorithm
slides.title: 2. Uniform-Cost Search (UCS)
slides.text:
2. Uniform-Cost Search (UCS)
•  UCS is an optimal graph search algorithm.
   Instead of expanding nodes level-by-level,
    it prioritizes vertices based on the lowest
   cumulative cost from the start vertex.

                Cost: Distance (in km)
•  Mathematical Notation: Minimizes f(v)=g(v),
  where g(v) is the cumulative cost (distance) from the
   start to the current vertex v.
•  Data Structures: It uses a priority queue ordered
   from smallest to largest value of g(v).



                                                                                                            25

visualInspection.notes: UCS lowest cumulative g(v), f(v)=g(v), distance units km and priority queue. Unqualified optimal assertion needs finite/nonnegative-cost/repeated-state/goal-removal conditions when generalized beyond this positive graph. Existing priority question covers defining rule. Footer 25.

slides.title: 3. A-Star
slides.text:
3. A-Star
•  The A* (A-star) search algorithm is a widely used
   graph search technique in robot navigation that
   finds the optimal path between two points by
   using a heuristic to guide its search.

•  Mathematical Notation: Minimizes f(v)=g(v)+h(v),
   where:
   – g(v) is the path cost from the start to vertex v
      (cost-to-come).
   – h(v) is a heuristic estimating the distance from v
      to the goal (cost-to-go).



                                                                                                            32

visualInspection.notes: A* f=g+h with cost-to-come g and estimated remaining h. Heuristic labels A7,B6,C5,D4,E3,F2,G0; road weights unchanged. Existing question covers g/h meanings; full-vector admissibility has not yet been tested. Footer 32.

slides.lectureTitle: Path planning, Graph Searches, and the A* Algorithm
slides.title: 3. A-Star
slides.text:
3. A-Star
•  The performance and accuracy of A* depend critically on the choice of the heuristic
   function:
➢Admissibility: A* is guaranteed to find the lowest-cost path only if the heuristic is
   "admissible," meaning it never overestimates the actual cost of reaching the goal.
  A non-admissible heuristic may lead to a non-optimal path.
➢Common heuristic function Examples:
   – Minimum-Distance: The Euclidean distance is a standard admissible heuristic
      because it is the shortest possible path between two
       points and cannot be an overestimate. (this example)
   – Minimum-Time: The heuristic must represent the travel
      time at the maximum possible speed in the
      environment to remain admissible.


                                                                                                            33

visualInspection.notes: Admissibility text never overestimate, nonadmissible may be nonoptimal; Euclidean-distance lower bound and minimum time at maximum possible speed. Additional implementation assumptions needed for general graph-search guarantee; costs and heuristic must share units. Existing four approved items cover definition, time lower bound, nonadmissible may-not-must and h=0. Footer 33.

These claims need compatible cost units and the stated physical motion model, not arbitrary unrelated edge costs.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary

•  Path planning = finding a safe, optimal route from start to goal.
•  Planning architecture: perception + localization → planning → execution.
•  Global planning (offline, full map) vs. local planning (real-time, reactive)
•  Environments represented as grid maps or graph-based maps.
•  BFS: fewest hops, but ignores cost — not always optimal.
•  UCS: guarantees shortest path, but explores many nodes.
•  A*: uses heuristic to reach optimal path faster than
  UCS





                                                                                                          37

visualInspection.notes: Summary repeats architecture perception+localization→planning→execution, global/local, maps and algorithms. Last A* faster-than-UCS statement is not a universal wall-clock guarantee; h=0 and heuristic-evaluation cost qualify it. Existing four summary questions are preserved, with possible new performance qualification only. Footer 37.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: The robot estimates its exact position relative to the map.
sourceIssues.qualification: Use the output as an estimate, not a promise of zero uncertainty.
sourceIssues.method: Distinguish the meaning of estimation from a guarantee of exactness; the source supplies no zero-noise or perfect-model assumption.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: Global planning computes an optimal path offline before movement starts.
sourceIssues.qualification: Treat this as the lecture’s comparison, not a universal prohibition on online global replanning.
sourceIssues.method: Apply the explicitly supplied whole-map replanning scenario and separate spatial planning scope from execution timing.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: Edge weights help determine the absolute best path based on real-world constraints.
sourceIssues.qualification: Best means minimum modeled cost for the declared objective and feasible represented routes, not every objective at once.
sourceIssues.method: Compare two different meanings of the edge weights explicitly listed by the source.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: Randomly hopping between neighboring vertices has no guarantee of reaching the goal.
sourceIssues.qualification: The generic warning must be distinguished from this particular finite directed acyclic graph, whose every A-started outgoing walk reaches E.
sourceIssues.method: Enumerate the five directed A-to-E paths and observe that all branches terminate at E within four moves.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: UCS is an optimal graph-search algorithm.
sourceIssues.qualification: The lecture’s positive-distance example satisfies the required nonnegative-edge setting. Do not extend the guarantee to arbitrary negative edge costs.
sourceIssues.method: Trace the fully specified acyclic negative-edge counterexample using the source’s cumulative-cost priority and goal-on-removal rule.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: A* uses a heuristic to reach the optimal path faster than UCS.
sourceIssues.qualification: The example establishes an expansion-count advantage, not an unconditional elapsed-time guarantee.
sourceIssues.method: Compare the printed node counts and equal route costs, then use f=g when h=0 as a counterexample to universal strict search reduction.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: The illustrative pose panel’s small coordinate triad appears to label two axes Y.
sourceIssues.qualification: Treat the illustration as a pose-versus-point-cloud example, not a reliable rotation-frame definition. Position and angle numbers are illustrative, not a derived computation.
sourceIssues.method: Actual pixel inspection of the pose inset; no rotation is inferred from its ambiguous triad.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: Binary free cells and geometric 8-neighbor adjacency are described without specifying footprint inflation, unknown-cell treatment or corner cutting.
sourceIssues.qualification: Use the source’s binary convention as stated; supply any finite-body or corner-cutting policy explicitly rather than inventing a universal default.
sourceIssues.method: Compare the mapping bullets with the earlier physical-size constraint and the explicit assumptions of the new footprint/corner questions.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: Generic expansion adds unexplored neighbors without explicitly separating already scheduled frontier entries.
sourceIssues.qualification: The displayed BFS trace retains one queued E rather than appending E again. Distinguish discovered/frontier from expanded/closed.
sourceIssues.method: Compare the literal generic pseudocode with the D-expansion frontier shown on page 1109.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: The source says Expand G on goal removal but omits G from its reported explored count.
sourceIssues.qualification: Retain the established convention: count successor expansions, not the successful goal removal. Existing approved questions already disclose this convention.
sourceIssues.method: Compare printed explored-node lists with the final goal-removal step; no accepted question is modified.

sourceIssues.sourceClaim: The A-star prose states optimality in terms of an admissible heuristic without spelling out graph-search reopening/consistency conditions.
sourceIssues.qualification: Do not interpret admissibility as an unconditional theorem for every implementation. The supplied positive finite graph has an admissible, consistent heuristic, verified directly on all 18 directed edge uses.
sourceIssues.method: Compare all source heuristic labels with exact remaining costs, and test h(u)≤c(u,v)+h(v). General implementation conditions are explanatory qualifications, not asserted as printed course content.
